Expert-constrained integer scorecard calibration

This is an experimental research scorecard, not a validated diagnostic model. It is not deep learning. A small, constrained, interpretable optimizer was chosen to preserve the expert-selected rules and point scale. No claim of methodological novelty or guaranteed publication is made.

Data and preprocessing

The source workbook yielded 55 contiguous case blocks across seven worksheet labels. The migraine tab indicates 14 but contains 13 blocks. Cases are not verified unique patients. Labels are worksheet membership, not verified mutually exclusive diagnoses. The mappings are VMigraine → Migraine, NeuritisHypofunction → Neuritis, ScCD → Third Window, and Bilateral wkns → Bilateral. Clinical review must confirm these mappings.

Only exact normalized prompt and option matches to existing structured questionnaire items are retained. Unknown options, free text, dates accidentally stored in choice fields, conflicting single-choice answers, and questions absent from the app are omitted. Multi-choice options remain separate features. Hidden conditional answers and conflicting “none of the above” selections are removed consistently with browser import. Age and sex are displayed but not used as predictors. All omissions require source reconciliation before clinical analysis.

Score and prediction definition

For each category, matched signed rule weights are added. Category support is 100 × net points / total positive available points, clipped to 0–100%, displayed to one decimal. It is not a probability. The single highest displayed support is the predicted class; tied maxima or all-zero support are “Uncertain / tied” and counted as incorrect in label-agreement metrics. Other unrecorded diagnoses are not known negatives.

Integer baseline and constraints

The original workbook defaults are preserved verbatim. A separate integer baseline uses largest-remainder rounding within each category and sign group, preserving rounded positive totals and rounded negative magnitudes separately. Every nonzero rule retains its sign and at least one point magnitude. The current dataset satisfies these integer constraints.

Learning varies each integer baseline weight by at most max(1, round(0.25 × absolute baseline weight)). No rule, category, question, or answer is added or removed. Zero weights and explicit −100 rule-outs are fixed. Categories without labeled examples and rules without training matches are frozen at the rounded baseline. Pairwise one-point transfers within the same category and sign preserve both positive and negative totals exactly.

Objective and algorithm

The objective is class-balanced top-category error + 0.02 × class-balanced multiclass softmax cross-entropy + 0.002 × mean squared normalized displacement from the integer baseline. Displacement is divided by each rule’s allowed radius. Softmax logits are unrounded clipped support divided by a fixed temperature of 20. There are no learned intercepts or demographic features.

Deterministic pairwise coordinate descent visits rule-index pairs in order, tries −1 then +1 point transfers, and accepts strict objective improvements (tolerance 10−10). It stops when no move improves the objective or after 30 sweeps. This is a local search, not a globally optimal integer program. An initial loss-only objective reduced training label agreement; the objective was revised to prioritize that agreement. This development choice is disclosed rather than treated as preregistered.

Evaluation

The deployable experimental weights are fitted on all cases. Their training performance is resubstitution. A separate deterministic three-fold evaluation groups identical structured-answer profiles, including profiles across different labels, into the same fold. Largest groups are assigned first to minimize their labels’ existing fold counts, then fold size, with fold index as the final tie-breaker. Every fold refits the optimizer using only its training subset. The fold assignments and case-level predictions remain in the private local audit.

Only 50 distinct answer profiles exist. Grouping identical profiles reduces obvious duplicate leakage but cannot identify repeated people with different responses. These small folds and development-driven choices mean the results are exploratory, not an independent estimate of clinical performance. No hyperparameter search or independent test set was used. Concussion and Neurological Other have no labeled examples, so their class recall cannot be evaluated.

The application displays label agreement, macro recall, per-class counts, and an out-of-fold confusion matrix. The trained model must not be described as outperforming defaults on new patients: the current out-of-fold result is lower than baseline performance on the same cohort. See scikit-learn’s cross-validation guidance for why training performance alone is insufficient.

Reproducibility and privacy

The repository includes the extraction, shared scoring, training and test scripts. The exported aggregate report includes the source extraction hash, constraints, iterations, weights, metrics and fold sizes. To reproduce locally: extract the source workbook using scripts/prepare_cohort.py, then run scripts/train_model.cjs with the private extracted cohort JSON path. The browser and trainer share model-core.js. Scripts require Node.js, and extraction requires Python with openpyxl. Exact source workbook and private audit must be retained in approved local storage.

No patient case files or case-level predictions are hosted with the app. Imported files are read in browser memory. Only model weights and aggregate evaluation results are published. A shared access code is not a patient-data security boundary.

Before a journal submission

Resolve source ambiguities, establish participant identities and independent reference diagnoses, clarify multi-diagnosis labeling, obtain institutional research/privacy approvals, lock a protocol and validation plan, compare against appropriate baselines, assess uncertainty and subgroup performance, and evaluate an independent cohort. Review relevant prediction-model reporting guidance and prior art with the clinical/statistical team. This implementation is a reproducible prototype, not a completed publishable clinical study.
